text: It’s 2023. An employee asks the company’s new AI assistant, an LLM, about a customer contract.
Confident, and wrong. A model knows only its training data plus its prompt, and it never saw your contracts.
2020: researchers named the fix. Fetch relevant text first, then let the model answer from it: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG.
2023: companies rolled out chat assistants with context windows of 4.1K–200K tokens. Tool calling was new, so retrieval picked the paragraphs.
2024: Gemini 1.5 Pro’s window hit 2M tokens, the record. Retrieval got smarter: graphs, better chunks, reranking. Multi-step tool use still stumbled.
Late 2024–26: 1M-token windows became common (Llama 4 Scout claims 10M). Models now act as agents, and retrieval is one tool they choose. Last question.
Your team’s obvious fix: paste the whole company drive into the assistant’s prompt. Before you try it, make a prediction.
Your pick is locked. The drive is pasted in.
Wrong again. The policy is on the drive, but truncation cut the paste before it.
It already overflows at 50 MB. Real company drives are much bigger.
5 TB is about 1.25T tokens. No model reads that in one go, and size is only one problem.
Even text that fits gets used badly: facts lost in the middle of a long prompt are often missed.
A prompt is a snapshot. Documents change every day.
And one prompt for everyone ignores permissions. Retrieval can filter per user. One question to finish.
Meet the assistant: for now just an LLM, with no documents wired in. A support lead asks it about refunds.
Made up. It sounds sure, but it has never read your refund policy, so it invented one.
Still made up: the documents are there, but nothing carries the right ones to the model. A Retriever finds the passages that match. Predict first.
Your pick is locked.
Correct, and it cites the policy it used: a grounded answer. That is RAG: Retrieve the passages, Augment the prompt, Generate the answer.
These passages reached the model, each with a similarity score.
The retriever compares the meaning of your question with every passage and keeps the closest. One question to finish.
The team now cuts documents into 16-word chunks and sends only the best.
Wrong, and sure of itself. The policy excludes enterprise contracts, but only one 16-word chunk reached the model. Predict what it held.
Your pick is locked. Open up the pipeline. First layer: the Chunker cuts every document into chunks before any search.
There it is: a cut after “does NOT”, the red mark. The rule and its exception landed in different chunks.
The Embedder turns each chunk into an embedding, 384 numbers for its meaning; the vector index stores them.
The map is a picture; ranking uses the true score. Last layer: the Context assembler packs chunks into the prompt.
Puzzle: the chunk the model gets ends on “does NOT”. Overlap repeats each chunk’s end in the next.
Correct, with a citation. With overlap the whole sentence sits in one chunk, so the model reads the exception. One question to finish.
Your pipeline from the last chapter is live. A consultant booking a trip asks the assistant about the hotel limit.
Wrong: $150 is from the retired 2018 travel policy. Before fixing anything, measure. The Evaluator judges the answer beside a retrieval meter.
Two meters. Recall@k: did the right sentence reach the model? Answer: was the reply right? Recall is 0%. Predict what fetching more will do.
Your pick is locked.
Recall hit 100%, yet the answer is still wrong: the retired 2018 policy came along.
Correct, citing the 2025 policy. Filters act before ranking, so stale text never competes.
Puzzle: a warehouse lead types “it’s broken again, who do I even call?”. Nothing in the documents reads like that.
Correct. The rewrite names a Portal outage outside business hours, so the Duty Desk rule ranks in: recall went 0% to 100%.
Puzzle: top-k is how many chunks the retriever hands over. At 1, the dock-door safety rule never arrives.
Past 6, recall stays 100% but the answer turns NOT FOUND. The model loses facts in the middle of long context.
Puzzle: a teammate set top-k to 10 “to be safe”, burying the rule mid-context.
Correct, and recall never moved: the rule was retrieved all along, only its position changed.
Puzzle: asked how long card data is kept, the assistant quotes a look-alike note about demo data.
Correct. Keyword matching rewards the real policy’s exact terms, so it outranks the look-alike.
Puzzle: the refund-window sentence is sliced in two, so the model finds no clear answer.
Correct. Overlap repeats each chunk’s end at the start of the next, so a sentence near a cut survives whole.
Puzzle, the last one: only one chunk is sent, and the fixed-size chunker cuts the lodging rule mid-sentence.
Correct. Seven levers, and the two meters told you which side to fix. One question to finish.
Every pipeline so far searched once: naive RAG, then advanced. Here the retriever sends one 16-word chunk, so each type’s strengths show.
Each run adds a row to the results strip under the canvas.
Wrong: one chunk stopped after “does NOT”. Agentic RAG puts an agent between retriever and model to decide whether to search again.
The agent sits in the side bay, wired to the retriever both ways. Max calls caps its retrievals.
Correct in 2 calls: the first chunk was cut mid-sentence, so the agent fetched its neighbours.
Both wrong, and the agent paid for a second search. Searching more never removes the retired 2018 policy: a metadata filter does. One question.
Harder: who approves purchases for the team owning the Kestrel K2 scanner integration? It spans two documents.
Not found either way: no single sentence links the scanner to the approver. GraphRAG walks a knowledge graph drawn from the documents.
The graph starts from what your question names, the Kestrel K2, and follows relations outward to the sentences behind them.
Still not found. One hop reached Fulfillment Systems, the team that owns the integration, and stopped short of its approver.
Correct: the second hop reached Tomasz Rehnquist in another document. The price: the walk sent about two dozen chunks instead of one. One question.
Next, a trap: how long does Larkspur keep customer payment card data? A meeting note about fake demo cards uses near-identical words.
Wrong: it read the demo note. Self-correcting RAG grades retrieval before answering, retries, and says “I don’t know” if nothing passes.
The Evaluator scores each search with a cross-encoder, which reads question and chunk together. A best chunk of 6 or more passes.
The look-alike and a rewrite both failed the bar, so it said “I don’t know”. No grade reads tables, PDFs or images.
A plain-text reader skips tables and images, so the Docs block’s three parsers start off.
Not found: the price list is a table, and with table parsing off retrieval never sees it.
Correct: $410, from the table’s K2 row. The sensor warranty sits in a vendor PDF, the lead in an org chart image.
Every block from chapters 3 to 6 is here, wired; the graph answers the module’s hardest question.
Now it is yours: drag blocks, wire them from their yellow knobs, click a wire to cut it.
Last stop. Five teams at Larkspur each describe a problem. Pick the RAG type that fits each one best.
